title: the wire: ACP as an agent, MCP as a server, MCP as a client
intent: The ACP handlers are pure functions with no process around them, and the MCP registry holds nine tools with placeholder handlers. Both reference harnesses are MCP clients, and this project is an MCP server: that is the complement, not the overlap. This wave is the wire: an ACP process speaking JSON-RPC over stdio, an MCP server publishing the registry, and an MCP client so that Yeah can use the tools of other agents as well as offer its own.
checks: ./scripts/dev ert tests/unit/test-yeah-state.el tests/unit/test-yeah-loop.el tests/unit/test-yeah-tools.el tests/unit/test-yeah-perm.el tests/unit/test-yeah-session.el tests/unit/test-yeah-compact.el tests/unit/test-yeah-undo.el tests/unit/test-yeah-acp.el tests/unit/test-yeah-emcp.el tests/unit/test-yeah-gptel.el tests/unit/test-yeah-subagent.el tests/unit/test-yeah-shell.el tests/unit/test-yeah-codes.el tests/unit/test-yeah-mcp.el tests/unit/test-yeah-mcp-client.el
objection: Publishing the tools of Emacs to the world is a promise about trust, and the trust boundary of a server is the client that calls it. The answer is not to publish less forever but to publish read-only by default and to make widening the surface an explicit decision of the operator, recorded in the same registry that the schema is bound to.
refuted_by: A client that can call the published tools of Emacs is by definition able to read everything the person can read. If the published surface can be widened without a decision, the decision is not a decision.
note: The stdio server answers one request at a time: a cancel that arrives while a prompt is running is read after that prompt reaches a terminal state, not in the middle of it. The check proves the framing, the routing and the answers; it does not prove preemption, and the map does not claim it.
